title: Nineteen Years Later, Yuvraj's Six Sixes Still Define T20 Cricket
excerpt: On September 19, 2007, an angry Yuvraj Singh took Stuart Broad apart at Kingsmead — and gave a young format its signature moment.
body:
• Nineteen years ago today, on September 19, 2007, Yuvraj Singh hit six sixes in one Stuart Broad over at Kingsmead, Durban, during the inaugural T20 World Cup.
  • The 19th-over assault followed a heated on-field exchange with England all-rounder Andrew Flintoff.
  • His 12-ball half-century remains the fastest fifty in T20 internationals; he finished 58 off 16 as India beat England by 18 runs.
  • On the 19th anniversary, Yuvraj shared a throwback video noting the feat began with Dimitri Mascarenhas hitting him for five sixes in an ODI two weeks earlier.

September 19 is cricket's most celebrated anniversary. Nineteen years ago today, at Kingsmead in Durban, Yuvraj Singh turned one over of cricket into folklore — six deliveries, six sixes, and a sport changed forever.

The stage was the inaugural ICC World Twenty20. India, having lost to New Zealand, were playing England in a must-win Super Eight fixture. Yuvraj walked in with India well placed — and then, between overs, got into a verbal exchange with England all-rounder Andrew Flintoff. England captain Paul Collingwood handed the 19th over to a 21-year-old Stuart Broad. What followed became the most famous over in T20 history.

Six deliveries, six sixes

Broad's first ball sailed over midwicket. The second went over backward square leg. The third and fourth cleared deep extra cover. The fifth went over midwicket again. And the sixth — launched over long-on — sealed the sequence: 36 runs off six legal balls.

The over also delivered a world record: Yuvraj reached his half-century in just 12 balls, a mark that still stands as the fastest fifty in T20 internationals. He finished with 58 off 16 deliveries, with seven sixes and three fours. India posted 218-4 and beat England by 18 runs.

"It was obviously a pretty tough day. I learnt a lot, I pretty much based a whole mental routine through that experience."

— Stuart Broad

A sport finds its signature moment

At the time, T20 cricket was still an unproven format, barely four years old and viewed with suspicion by traditionalists. Yuvraj's over — the first time a batter had hit six sixes in an over in a T20 international, per the ICC — gave the young format its defining highlight reel. It was audacity that fit the format's promise: anything, it seemed, was possible in 20 overs.

There is an irony Yuvraj himself flagged on the 19th anniversary, sharing a throwback video on social media. "It all started with this," he wrote — pointing to Dimitri Mascarenhas smashing him for five consecutive sixes in an ODI barely two weeks earlier. From the receiving end of an assault to the author of a greater one, inside a fortnight.

The long shadow of one over

Broad, 21 at the time, has spoken about how the over shaped him. He called it "a pretty tough day" and said he rushed his preparation and lacked any pre-ball routine — lessons that became the foundation of his "warrior mode." The incident, he said, "steeled me up to make me the competitor I am to this day." He went on to become one of England's greatest-ever fast bowlers.

Yuvraj, meanwhile, powered India to the inaugural title under MS Dhoni, and four years later became the first all-rounder to score more than 300 runs and take 15 wickets in a single World Cup, winning Player of the Tournament in India's 2011 triumph.

Why it endures

For the Indian diaspora, the over is a shared cultural timestamp — fans across the US, UK, Canada and Australia can tell you exactly where they were when ball number six cleared long-on. It remains the high-water mark of individual T20 brilliance, even as the format has exploded into the world's most lucrative cricket economy. Records have tumbled around it, but the 12-ball fifty has survived nineteen years of power-hitting evolution.

What to watch next

This week of all weeks, the past and present of T20 batting sit side by side: India's current generation, under Gautam Gambhir, is chasing the format's first-ever 300-run innings score. Nineteen years after Yuvraj set the standard for one over, his successors are trying to set one for twenty.
